newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ shares and bonds surge on low inflation figures.
newsitem.headline: NZ shares and bonds surge on low inflation figures.

text.p: Lower-than-expected inflation figures unleashed a flood of buying in New Zealand shares and bonds on Tuesday, but comments from nationalist power-broker Winston Peters pushed the kiwi dollar down.
The Consumer Price Index rose 0.6 percent in the September quarter and 2.4 percent for the year to September, against expectations of a 2.6 percent rise.
The outcome prompted heavy buying in the interest rate markets as dealers anticipated a formal easing of monetary policy by the central Reserve Bank later this year.

The enthusiasm further fuelled a rally in shares, despite the inconclusive result of Saturday's general election. The top-40 index closed at 2,321.66, a rise of 2.53 percent and its highest point in 32 months.

"There has been a lot of tension in the market for a number of weeks, for both political and inflation reasons, and it's like a valve that has been released over the last 48 hours," ASB Bank Economist Anthony Byett said.

Political parties met in Wellington for the first time since the election, which left nationalist New Zealand First holding the balance of power between the conservative National Party and the centre-left Labour Party.

NZ First leader Winston Peters sent the kiwi dollar into a spin by telling a news conference it was overvalued. His comment that it may take until Christmas for a coalition to form did not augur well for certainty in the forex market, dealers said.
The Kiwi, already weakened by the prospect of lower interest rates, ended at US$0.6965, down sharply from its 0.6995 opening and overnight high of 0.7018.
One Auckland dealer said there was increased nervousness over Peters. "At the end of the day comments like that show he's a bit of a loose cannon," he said.

Rating agency Standard and Poor's issued a reassuring commentary on the election. It reaffirmed New Zealand's credit ratings and said it did not expect any economic policy changes that would damage them.
Markets broadly have taken an upbeat view of the election result, largely because the far-left Alliance polled poorly.

The December bank bill futures closed up 33 basis points at 90.99, just slightly off their peak of 91.01. Total turnover in the bank bill futures was 10,236, the highest ever. Ninety-day bank bill rates fell about 28 basis points to 9.56 percent.
Finance Minister Bill Birch sought to poor cold water on the rally, warning people not to get over excited about a single set of inflation numbers.
But he said the CPI outcome would improve confidence in the Reserve Bank's ability to hit its zero to two percent inflation target over the next 12 months.
New Zealand First and the National Party, which remains as caretaker government, held separate meetings on how coalition negotiations should proceed.

National and Labour have both said they aim to form a government with NZ First support, and analysts on balance see a Labour-led coalition as the more likely. But Peters said the chances of NZ First joinining with either party were 50/50.
